title: Private Deployments - VPC & On-Prem Deployment Guide, Day-2 Ops, Upgrades, and Customer Requirements Library
author: Priya Sharma
content:
Summary:
This document consolidates guidance for Redwood Inference private deployments: VPC and on-prem packaging, reference architectures for single-rack and hybrid-cloud deployments, day‑2 operational procedures (monitoring, backups, scaling, incident handling), and upgrade & rollback playbooks. It also catalogs the common customer requirements we ship against (networking, security, compliance, capacity). The goal is a single reference for engineers, solutions architects, and SREs planning and operating customer private deployments.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: VPC-based customer-managed deployments, on‑prem (air‑gapped) packaging & installation, day‑2 operations, upgrade/rollback procedures, and the customer requirements library.
- Audience: Solutions Engineering, Private Deployments Engineering, SRE, Customer Success, and Security/Compliance reviewers.

1) High-level deployment patterns
We support three common private deployment topologies:
A. VPC (cloud customer VPC) — recommended for most customers that want managed networking and KMS integration.
B. On‑prem single-rack (air‑gapped or limited egress) — used by regulated customers or those with strict data residency.
C. Hybrid (on‑prem GPU cluster + cloud control plane or burst to cloud) — for customers needing local inference with cloud-based control/observability.

Reference architectures (descriptive diagrams included inline):
- VPC Reference (Recommended):
  - Control plane (Redwood-managed) communicates to a customer VPC via a dedicated VPC peering / PrivateLink or Site-to-Site VPN depending on network policies.
  - Worker cluster lives in private subnets with NAT or egress via managed gateway for image pulls (or airgap alternative).
  - KMS/HSM connectivity over private endpoint for encryption keys.
  - Recommended subnets: three AZs, each with at least 1 GPU node for HA.

- On‑Prem Single‑Rack:
  - Full on‑prem installation with local registry, NFS/CSI-backed model store, and optional airgap tarball for installs.
  - Control plane can be deployed as a customer-managed control plane or linked to Redwood’s control plane via an outbound-only, customer-approved relay.

- Hybrid:
  - Local inference nodes for low-latency workloads, with model catalog and metrics forwarded (optionally) to Redwood-managed observability buckets. Burst to cloud via secure peering for overflow.

2) Pre‑deployment checklist (minimum required configuration)
Table: Minimum customer requirements (summary)
| Area | Requirement | Recommended value / notes | Owner |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Network | Private subnets (3 AZs) + routing | 3 AZs, /24 per subnet recommended | Customer network team |
| DNS | Internal DNS + split horizon for control endpoints | FQDNs supplied by Redwood | Customer infra |
| IAM | Service accounts, RBAC mapping, KMS access policy | Policy template provided | Security / Infra |
| Storage | 5–10 TB model store (NFS/CSI) | Depends on model mix — adjust with Solutions ENG | Customer infra |
| GPU capacity | 1–8 A100/ H100 (initial) | Size to match QPS/SLA — see sizing guide section | Customer infra / Solutions ENG |
| Bandwidth | 1 Gbps+ between control plane and workers | For high-throughput customers consider 10 Gbps | Customer network |
| Egress | Image pull path OR airgap tarball | Airgap recommended for classified environments | Customer infra / Solutions ENG |

3) Packaging and installation options
- Kubernetes (preferred): Helm chart + operator for lifecycle. Provides standard upgrade path and health checks.
- Docker Compose / systemd (small PoCs): for single-rack PoC. Not recommended for production.
- Airgap tarball: includes container images, Helm chart, CRDs, and model artifacts for environments with no outbound access.

Packaging artifacts we provide:
- helm/redwood-inference-chart-<version>.tgz
- airgap/redwood-airgap-<version>.tar.gz (includes registry images and install scripts)
- packages/redwood-onprem-<version>.rpm and .deb (for OS-level installer)

Sample Helm install (Kubernetes, values.yaml excerpt):
# values.yaml (snippet)
replicaCount: 2
image:
  registry: internal-registry.example.com
  tag: v2026.11.20
nodeSelector:
  accelerator: nvidia-a100
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "8"
    memory: "32Gi"
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: "1"
persistence:
  modelStore:
    enabled: true
    size: 5Ti

Install command (example):
helm install redwood ./redwood-inference-chart-2026.11.20.tgz -f values.yaml --namespace redwood

Airgap install notes:
- Validate checksum of tarball.
- Load images into local registry: "ctr images import /path/to/images.tar" or "docker load -i images.tar".
- Apply Helm chart pointing to local registry URL and set imagePullSecrets.

4) Day‑2 operations (runbook-style guidance)
Operational goals: maintain SLOs, ensure safe upgrades, and efficient capacity scaling.
Key responsibilities:
- Customer infra owns physical hardware, network, and KMS connectivity.
- Redwood Private Deployments team owns the application manifests, operator, and upgrade artifacts for supported releases.

Monitoring & alerting (minimum set):
- Metrics to collect: request_latency_p95, request_failure_rate, gpu_utilization, kv_cache_size, model_load_time, pod_restart_total.
- Alerts (examples):
  - request_failure_rate > 1% for 10m -> P1 to oncall SRE
  - request_latency_p95 > SLO (see SLOs section) for 5m -> page SRE
  - gpu_utilization > 95% for 5m -> recommend scale-up or redistribute workloads

Logging and traces:
- Structured logs (JSON) shipped to customer log sink or Redwood-managed observability per agreement.
- Trace sampling: default 10% for customers, adjustable with Solutions ENG.

Backup and model store snapshotting:
- Periodic snapshot of model store metadata (daily) and tarball of active model artifacts (weekly) in customer's approved storage.
- Store KV cache checkpoints only for large models where restart time exceeds allowed maintenance window.

Scaling and capacity management:
- Horizontal scaling: increase replicaCount for stateless frontends and add GPU nodes for model workers.
- Autoscaler settings: we recommend cluster-autoscaler with threshold-based rules tied to GPU utilization > 70% sustained for 10m.
- Capacity planning cadence: monthly review for production customers, weekly for customers with >50% cluster growth.

Common day‑2 procedures (numbered playbook):
1. Replace a failed GPU node
   - cordon node: kubectl cordon <node>
   - drain workloads: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
   - reprovision at infra layer, verify GPU drivers and nvidia-container-runtime
   - uncordon: kubectl uncordon <node>
2. Add capacity for burst
   - validate network throughput and quotas
   - add nodes using Terraform or cloud console
   - verify cluster autoscaler pick-up and update Helm values if necessary
3. Restore model store from snapshot
   - validate snapshot integrity (SHA256)
   - rsync or restore objects to model store path
   - restart model service pods in rolling fashion: kubectl rollout restart deployment/model-service

5) Upgrade and rollback procedures (safe, tested choreography)
Upgrade principles:
- Always perform upgrades in a staging environment that mirrors production (node types, network, model mix).
- Use canary or blue/green strategies for control plane and model-serving shards.
- Back up model store metadata, database (if present), and operator CRs prior to any schema migration.

Step-by-step upgrade (example Helm/operator upgrade):
1. Create release branch and tag artifacts (operator, helm chart, images).
2. Notify stakeholders and schedule maintenance window (if needed).
3. Run pre-upgrade checks: health endpoints, CR integrity, disk pressure, and snapshot creation.
4. Deploy canary: upgrade 1 of N replicas in a non-critical AZ / node pool. Run smoke tests for 10–30 minutes.
5. Gradual rollout: increase percentage of upgraded replicas (25% -> 50% -> 100%) while monitoring key metrics.
6. Post-upgrade validation: functional tests, perf tests, model load times, and production traffic holdback checks.

Rollback checklist (if upgrade causes degradation):
- Immediately stop rollout and revert operator version via Helm: helm rollback <release> <revision>.
- If DB schema was migrated and incompatible, follow the documented DB rollback in the migration guide (consult Redwood migrations team).
- Re-deploy previous images and re-apply previous Helm values.
- Validate system stabilization before re-scheduling another upgrade.

6) Incident response and triage for private deployments
- Triage steps: collect cluster diagnostics (kubectl get events, pod logs, node metrics), model service logs, and recent change list.
- Escalation matrix: Solutions ENG -> Private Deployments Eng -> SRE -> Product Security (for security incidents).
- Post-incident: produce an incident summary with root cause, timeline, mitigation, and follow-ups (owner and ETA).

7) SLOs and performance expectations (default):
- Latency SLOs: p50 < 100ms, p95 < 500ms for short prompts (<256 tokens) on dedicated A100/H100-backed clusters with appropriate tuning.
- Availability: 99.9% monthly SLA (for Dedicated/private customers with an SLA add-on).
- Model load time: < 30s for warmed cache models, < 2m for cold start for large 70B+ models (varies by quantization/profile).

8) Customer requirements library (common asks and standard responses)
- Requirement: Air‑gap install. Response: We provide an airgap tarball with install instructions and a local registry import script; offline verification steps included.
- Requirement: FIPS / HSM integrations. Response: We support customer-managed KMS via private endpoints; provide HSM integration patterns and KMS policy templates.
- Requirement: Data residency & audit logs. Response: Audit logging can be forwarded to the customer SIEM; retention policy configurable; provide evidence folder and schema for compliance review.
- Requirement: Deterministic model outputs. Response: We document and expose seed and sampling configuration options; deterministic mode supported for unit tests.
- Requirement: Restricted outbound connectivity. Response: Airgap install or outbound-only relay architecture; provide hardened egress proxy patterns.

9) Ownership, contacts, and escalation
- Primary owners: Private Deployments Eng (team: private-deployments@redwood.ai), Oncall SRE (rotation info in PagerDuty).
- Security contact: security-ops@redwood.ai for incidents involving keys, secrets, or exfiltration.
- For new customer engagements contact: solutions-eng@redwood.ai

Appendices
A. Sample terraform snippet (VPC peering):
resource "aws_vpc_peering_connection" "peer" {
  vpc_id = "var.redwood_vpc_id"
  peer_vpc_id = "var.customer_vpc_id"
  accepter {
    allow_remote_vpc_dns_resolution = true
  }
}

B. Upgrade checklist (quick)
- [ ] Backup model store metadata
- [ ] Snapshot DB (if applicable)
- [ ] Validate canary smoke tests pass for 30m
- [ ] Monitor p95 latency and error rate during rollout
- [ ] Post-upgrade perf regression check

C. Related artifacts and templates (links)
- Network policy templates (link)
- Helm values templates (link)
- Airgap verification checklist (link)
- DB migration playbook (link)

D. Glossary
- Control plane: Redwood-managed or customer-managed service that orchestrates model deployments, auth, and billing hooks.
- Model store: Persistent storage that contains model artifacts (weights, tokenizer).
- KV cache: Key-value cache for attention state used to speed repeated generation.
